evidence: Figure 5A shows stomatal closure in response to AS2 in wild type and ost1-2 sal1-8.

claim: ost1-2 does not respond to AS2 or ABA.
source: AS2 induced stomatal closure to a similar extent as ABA in both wild type and ost1-2 sal1-8, while ost1-2 did not respond to either AS2 or ABA as expected (Figure 5A).
evidence: Figure 5A shows lack of stomatal closure in response to AS2 and ABA in ost1-2.

claim: ABA signaling and downstream molecular responses mediated through dimeric, and possibly some monomeric, ABA receptors are active when PAP levels are elevated.
source: Hence, ABA signaling and downstream molecular responses mediated through dimeric, and possibly some monomeric, ABA receptors are active when PAP levels are elevated.
evidence: This is inferred from the AS2 experiment showing that PAP can restore ABA signaling through specific PYR/PYL receptors.

claim: Loss of SAL1 restores turgor in the ost1 (snrk2.6) snrk2.2 snrk2.3 triple mutant.
source: Significantly, loss of SAL1 restored turgor in the absence of all SnRKs (Figure 5B), which would suggest the other SnRK2s are not compensating for the loss of OST1 in ost1-2 sal1-8.
evidence: Figure 5B shows photos of the quadruple mutant with restored turgor.

claim: CDPK32 and CDPK34 activate SLAC1 anion currents in Xenopus laevis oocytes.
source: In Xenopus laevis oocytes, strong and significant activation of SLAC1 anion currents were elicited upon co-expression of CDPK32 or CDPK34 with SLAC1 compared to non-kinase injected or water injected controls (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Figure 5C shows SLAC1 activation by CDPK32 and CDPK34 in oocytes.

claim: CRK2 and CRK8 activate SLAC1 comparable to that by OST1 in Xenopus laevis oocytes.
source: CRK2 and CRK8 also activated SLAC1 comparable to that by OST1 (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Figure 5D shows SLAC1 activation by CRK2 and CRK8 in oocytes.

claim: CDPK34 is expressed in ost1-2 sal1-8 guard cells.
source: Consistent with these results, CDPK34 is expressed in ost1-2 sal1-8 guard cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and guard cell expression is already reported for CDPK32, CRK2 and CRK8 (Yang et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011; Boudsocq and Sheen, 2013).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1B shows in situ PCR detection of CDPK34 in guard cells.

claim: Guard cell expression is reported for CDPK32, CRK2 and CRK8.
source: Consistent with these results, CDPK34 is expressed in ost1-2 sal1-8 guard cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and guard cell expression is already reported for CDPK32, CRK2 and CRK8 (Yang et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011; Boudsocq and Sheen, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PAP does not increase [Ca2+]cyt transients in guard cells.
source: During our measurements we observed cells with spontaneous [Ca2+]cyt increases and cells without [Ca2+]cyt transients, which were consistent with previous observations (Grabov and Blatt, 1998; Staxen et al., 1999). These fluctuations clustered into three types of oscillation patterns, but significantly in none of these were [Ca2+]cyt transients increased by PAP (Figure 6).
evidence: Figure 6 shows Ca2+ oscillation patterns in guard cells treated with PAP.

claim: PAP-mediated closure relies on a sufficient concentration of Ca2+.
source: Since PAP up-regulated multiple Ca2+ signaling proteins but does not influence calcium transients, we investigated whether PAP instead requires Ca2+. Indeed, PAP-mediated closure relied on a sufficient concentration of Ca2+ (Figure 7A) and was prevented by addition of intracellular and extracellular Ca2+ chelators (Figure 7B).
evidence: Figure 7A shows dependence of PAP-mediated stomatal closure on Ca2+ concentration.

claim: PAP-mediated closure is prevented by addition of intracellular and extracellular Ca2+ chelators.
source: Since PAP up-regulated multiple Ca2+ signaling proteins but does not influence calcium transients, we investigated whether PAP instead requires Ca2+. Indeed, PAP-mediated closure relied on a sufficient concentration of Ca2+ (Figure 7A) and was prevented by addition of intracellular and extracellular Ca2+ chelators (Figure 7B).
evidence: Figure 7B shows inhibition of PAP-mediated stomatal closure by Ca2+ chelators.

claim: The kinetics and extent of PAP-mediated closure in leaf peels are attenuated compared to ABA by low exogenous calcium in the treatment buffer.
source: Also, the kinetics and extent of PAP-mediated closure in leaf peels were attenuated compared to ABA by low exogenous calcium in the treatment buffer (Figure 7C).
evidence: Figure 7C shows attenuated PAP-mediated stomatal closure under low Ca2+ conditions.

claim: Inhibiting ROS production by NADPH oxidases using DPI inhibits PAP-mediated stomatal closure.
source: Inhibiting ROS production by NADPH oxidases using the NADPH oxidase inhibitor diphenyleneiodonium (DPI) inhibited PAP-mediated stomatal closure (Figure 7D).
evidence: Figure 7D shows inhibition of PAP-mediated stomatal closure by DPI.

claim: PAP is elevated in dry seeds of sal1-6 compared to wild type.
source: We quantified PAP in dry seeds of sal1-6 and it is indeed elevated compared to wild type (Figure 8A).
evidence: Figure 8A shows PAP quantification in seeds.

claim: sal1-6 freshly-harvested seeds have increased dormancy compared to wild type.
source: In freshly-harvested seeds, sal1-6 had increased dormancy compared to wild type (Figure 8B).
evidence: Figure 8B shows delayed germination in fresh sal1-6 seeds.

claim: After-ripened sal1-6 seeds germinate slower than similarly treated wild type seeds.
source: Furthermore, sal1-6 seeds that were after-ripened at room temperature to break seed dormancy still germinated slower than similarly treated wild type seeds (Figure 8C).
evidence: Figure 8C shows delayed germination in after-ripened sal1-6 seeds.

claim: Exogenous ABA and paclobutrazol have no significant effect on abi1-1 germination rates.
source: As expected exogenous ABA and paclobutrazol had no significant effect on abi1-1 germination rates, but ABA responsiveness was restored in abi1-1 sal1-8, albeit not to the same extent as wild type (Figure 8E).
evidence: Figure 8E shows lack of germination inhibition in abi1-1 in response to ABA and paclobutrazol.

claim: ABA responsiveness is restored in abi1-1 sal1-8 seeds, albeit not to the same extent as wild type.
source: As expected exogenous ABA and paclobutrazol had no significant effect on abi1-1 germination rates, but ABA responsiveness was restored in abi1-1 sal1-8, albeit not to the same extent as wild type (Figure 8E).
evidence: Figure 8E shows partial restoration of germination inhibition in abi1-1 sal1-8 in response to ABA and paclobutrazol.

claim: PAP treatment significantly represses wild type germination in combination with ABA and paclobutrazol in a dose-dependent manner.
source: PAP treatment significantly repressed wild type and abi1-1 germination in combination with ABA and paclobutrazol in a dose-dependent manner, but not by itself.
evidence: Figure 8F-G shows dose-dependent germination inhibition by PAP in combination with ABA and paclobutrazol.

claim: PAP treatment significantly represses abi1-1 germination in combination with ABA and paclobutrazol in a dose-dependent manner.
source: PAP treatment significantly repressed wild type and abi1-1 germination in combination with ABA and paclobutrazol in a dose-dependent manner, but not by itself.
evidence: Figure 8F-G shows dose-dependent germination inhibition by PAP in combination with ABA and paclobutrazol.

claim: PAP treatment does not significantly repress germination by itself.
source: PAP treatment significantly repressed wild type and abi1-1 germination in combination with ABA and paclobutrazol in a dose-dependent manner, but not by itself.
evidence: Figure 8F shows that PAP alone does not significantly inhibit germination.

claim: Combinatorial treatments of PAP, ABA and paclobutrazol lower Col-0 germination from 100% to <20%.
source: The combinatorial treatments lowered Col-0 germination from 100% to <20% and for abi1-1 from 100% in the presence of 1 or 2 µM ABA to <50%.
evidence: Figure 8F-G shows germination rates under combinatorial treatments.

claim: Combinatorial treatments of PAP, ABA and paclobutrazol lower abi1-1 germination from 100% in the presence of 1 or 2 µM ABA to <50%.
source: The combinatorial treatments lowered Col-0 germination from 100% to <20% and for abi1-1 from 100% in the presence of 1 or 2 µM ABA to <50%.
evidence: Figure 8F-G shows germination rates under combinatorial treatments.

claim: PAP content in wild type seeds is seven-fold higher than in leaves.
source: Of interest was the observation that PAP content in wild type seeds was seven-fold higher than in leaves (Figure 8A).
evidence: Figure 8A shows PAP quantification in leaves and seeds.

claim: SAL1 transcript abundance in seeds is the lowest amongst all Arabidopsis developmental stages.
source: SAL1 transcript abundance in seeds is the lowest amongst all Arabidopsis developmental stages and dry seed imbibition increases SAL1 expression greater than 10-fold, constituting the most dramatic change in SAL1 expression across 3000 different perturbations (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B) (Zimmermann et al., 2004).
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1A shows SAL1 expression across developmental stages.

claim: Dry seed imbibition increases SAL1 expression greater than 10-fold.
source: SAL1 transcript abundance in seeds is the lowest amongst all Arabidopsis developmental stages and dry seed imbibition increases SAL1 expression greater than 10-fold, constituting the most dramatic change in SAL1 expression across 3000 different perturbations (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B) (Zimmermann et al., 2004).
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1B shows SAL1 expression changes during seed imbibition.

claim: The transition from dry seed to germinating seed constitutes the most dramatic change in SAL1 expression across 3000 different perturbations.
source: SAL1 transcript abundance in seeds is the lowest amongst all Arabidopsis developmental stages and dry seed imbibition increases SAL1 expression greater than 10-fold, constituting the most dramatic change in SAL1 expression across 3000 different perturbations (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B) (Zimmermann et al., 2004).
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1B shows SAL1 expression changes across perturbations.

claim: SAL1 protein abundance in seeds is substantially decreased compared to leaves.
source: Associated with the elevated PAP and lower SAL1 mRNA levels we did observe substantially decreased SAL1 protein abundance in seeds compared to leaves (Figure 8A).
evidence: Figure 8A shows Western blot of SAL1 protein in leaves and seeds.

claim: In seeds, PAP accumulation and signaling may be modulated by a downregulation of SAL1 abundance.
source: Therefore unlike leaves, in seeds PAP accumulation and signaling may be modulated by a downregulation of SAL1 abundance.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing decreased SAL1 mRNA and protein in seeds.
